about: Instruments, eyepieces and targets for the Telescope simulator (eyepiece.html). Apertures and focal lengths are typical of each class of instrument, not of any one product. Surface brightnesses (sb, V magnitudes per square arcsecond) are what the naked eye would receive; see eyepiece-optics.js for every formula and its source.

instruments.name: Your eyes
instruments.blurb: A 7 mm pupil, no magnification. The baseline everything else is compared with.
instruments.note: Your eye's pupil opens to about 7 mm in the dark (a little less as we get older). The circle shows a 12° patch of sky: about the width of your fist held at arm's length.

instruments.name: 10×50 binoculars
instruments.blurb: 10× magnification, 50 mm lenses. Wide, bright, right way up, and fits in a drawer.
instruments.note: Binoculars use prisms, so the view is the right way up. A 6.5° field shows whole star clusters that are too big for most telescopes.

instruments.name: 70 mm refractor
instruments.blurb: A lens at the front, on a light tripod: the classic beginner's telescope.
instruments.note: A 70 mm lens with a 700 mm focal length (f/10). Most refractors are used with a star diagonal, a mirror that makes viewing comfortable but shows the sky mirror-reversed.

instruments.name: 130 mm reflector
instruments.blurb: A mirror at the bottom of the tube. Collects 3.4× the light of a 70 mm lens.
instruments.note: A Newtonian reflector: 130 mm mirror, 650 mm focal length (f/5). Newtonians show the sky upside down (rotated 180°), which makes no difference in space.

instruments.name: 8-inch Dobsonian
instruments.blurb: A 203 mm mirror on a simple swivel box. The most-recommended first 'serious' telescope.
instruments.note: A Newtonian reflector on a Dobsonian mount: a wooden box that turns left-right and up-down by hand. 203 mm (8 inches), 1200 mm focal length (f/5.9).

instruments.name: 11-inch Schmidt-Cassegrain
instruments.blurb: A compact folded telescope, 280 mm across, usually on a motorised 'go-to' mount.
instruments.note: A Schmidt-Cassegrain telescope (SCT): a mirror plus a thin corrector lens folds 2800 mm of focal length (f/10) into a short tube. Used with a star diagonal, so the view is mirror-reversed.

instruments.name: 1 m observatory telescope
instruments.blurb: A research-class mirror under a dome. Some observatories hold public viewing nights.
instruments.note: A 1-metre Cassegrain at f/8. Mirrors this big are almost always limited by the air, not by their size: the extra aperture mostly buys brightness.

instruments.name: Hubble Space Telescope
instruments.blurb: A 2.4 m mirror above the air, in visible and ultraviolet light. Camera only: nobody looks through it.
instruments.note: The Hubble Space Telescope (HST) orbits above the atmosphere, so there is no twinkling and no light pollution. It has no eyepiece: its cameras take pictures. The square shows the 162″ field of its Wide Field Camera 3 (WFC3), at 500 nm (green light).

instruments.name: James Webb Space Telescope
instruments.blurb: A 6.5 m gold mirror, 1.5 million km away, seeing infrared (heat) light. Camera only.
instruments.note: The James Webb Space Telescope (JWST) sees infrared light, which our eyes cannot. It has no eyepiece: pictures are made in infrared and shown in 'false colour' (longer wavelengths drawn redder). The square shows 2.2′, one module of its Near Infrared Camera (NIRCam), at 2 micrometres (µm).

instruments.name: Your own telescope
instruments.blurb: Type in the aperture and focal length printed on any telescope.
instruments.note: Enter the two numbers printed on the tube or in the manual: aperture (the width of the main lens or mirror) and focal length.

targets.name: Moon
targets.eye: Craters line up along the terminator, the line between day and night, where long shadows show every bump. The full Moon is flat and dazzling.
targets.photo: Photos look much the same as the eye: the Moon is bright enough for the colour-seeing cones of your eye.
targets.tip: Best a few days either side of first or last quarter, not at full Moon.

targets.name: Jupiter
targets.eye: A small, bright disc with two dark belts and up to four 'stars' in a line: the moons Galileo found in 1610. They move from night to night, and Io visibly from hour to hour.
targets.photo: Planetary cameras record thousands of frames and keep the sharpest, showing far more than one glance.
targets.tip: About 50× shows the moons; 100–200× shows the belts.

targets.name: Saturn
targets.eye: The rings are the moment most people fall for astronomy. Around 2025–2026 they are close to edge-on, a thin line through the planet, opening up again over the next years.
targets.photo: Same shape, more colour and sharper detail from stacked video.
targets.tip: Any telescope from 70 mm shows the rings at 50× or more.

targets.name: Mars
targets.eye: Small and orange. Only near opposition, every 26 months, is Mars close enough to show a polar cap and dark markings.
targets.photo: Stacked video brings out the dark features and the white polar cap.
targets.tip: Wait for opposition (next: February 2027) and use high power on a steady night.

targets.name: Venus
targets.eye: Dazzling, featureless cloud tops, but it shows phases like the Moon: Galileo's proof that Venus orbits the Sun.
targets.photo: In ultraviolet, cameras catch faint cloud bands. In visible light it is just as plain.
targets.tip: Observe in twilight so it is not so glaring.

targets.name: Orion Nebula
targets.eye: A ghostly grey-green glow shaped like a bird with spread wings, around four hot stars called the Trapezium. It is the brightest nebula in the sky, but the eye still sees it without colour.
targets.photo: The famous pink and red come from hydrogen gas, glowing at a wavelength the dark-adapted eye barely registers: a long exposure collects it.
targets.tip: Low power (20–60×) and a dark sky. Visible in the evening from about December to March.

targets.name: Andromeda Galaxy
targets.eye: A soft oval smudge with a bright centre: the light of a trillion stars that left 2.5 million years ago. It is six full Moons long, but the eye sees mostly the core.
targets.photo: Photos show spiral dust lanes, blue star-forming regions and two companion galaxies (M32 and M110) across 3°: far wider than most telescope views.
targets.tip: Binoculars or the lowest power you have, from a dark site. Autumn evenings.

targets.name: Pleiades
targets.eye: A little dipper of blue-white stars, with dozens more appearing in binoculars. Too big for most telescopes at high power.
targets.photo: Long exposures reveal blue dust the cluster is passing through, lit like fog in headlights. The eye rarely sees it.
targets.tip: Binoculars are ideal. Autumn to spring evenings.

targets.name: Albireo
targets.eye: Gold and blue: the prettiest colour contrast in the sky. The two stars are 34″ apart, easy at 30× in any telescope.
targets.photo: The colours look the same: the stars are bright enough for colour vision.
targets.tip: Summer and autumn evenings, in the Swan (Cygnus).

targets.name: Epsilon Lyrae
targets.eye: Sharp eyes see two stars 3.5′ apart. A telescope splits each of those again, 2.3″ and 2.4″ apart: a classic test of resolution and steady air. The view starts on ε1; ε2 is 3.5′ to the south (drag to find it).
targets.photo: Same stars: this target is about sharpness, not colour.
targets.tip: About 100× or more with 70 mm or larger, on a steady night. Next to Vega.

targets.name: Sun
targets.eye: Through a certified white-light filter: a white disc darker at the edge, with dark sunspots that change day by day.
targets.photo: Special hydrogen-alpha filters show prominences and flares; see our Solar observatory page for today's Sun.
targets.tip: Only with a certified full-aperture solar filter over the FRONT of the telescope. Never an eyepiece filter.

galilean.note: Opposition magnitudes (Jupiter at 4.2 AU from Earth, 5.2 AU from the Sun), NASA Jupiter satellite fact sheet.
